title: An eclipse
hookLine: when the moon crosses the sun, people everywhere stop

cards: The light goes wrong first. It's the middle of the day, but the shadows get sharp and strange, and the color drains out of everything. Birds go quiet.
The air cools. On sidewalks and rooftops, people who were busy a minute ago stand still, faces tipped up, holding cardboard viewers or special glasses. Strangers talk to each other.
Somebody gasps. Then the light comes back, and everyone, a little sheepishly, goes back to what they were doing.

teach.h: THE MOON IS JUST IN THE WAY.
teach.b: First, what's happening. The moon passes between the earth and the sun and, for a stretch, blocks its light. The sun hasn't gone anywhere; the moon is just in the way.
Knowing that doesn't seem to spoil it. People who understand the science perfectly still stop and stare. Second, how a darkened sun once sounded.
In the Hebrew Bible, the prophet Joel uses it as a picture of a world turned upside down.

teach.h: JOEL: THE SUN TURNED INTO DARKNESS.
teach.b: In the King James words: "The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and the terrible day of the LORD come." For the prophet, a sun gone dark meant something huge was close.
Third, a correction from the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him.
According to a hadith in the collection of al-Bukhari, the sun was eclipsed on the day his young son Ibrahim died, and people said it was because of Ibrahim's death. The Prophet stopped them.

teach.h: NOT FOR ANYONE'S DEATH OR LIFE.
teach.b: The sun and the moon, he said, are two of God's signs, and they are not eclipsed for anyone's death or life. When you see it, pray and remember God. Muslim tradition keeps a special prayer for eclipses.
In the middle of his own grief, he refused to let the sky be read as a message about his family, and turned people from omens to prayer. Fourth, the thread.
Whether you read an eclipse as a sign from God, a reminder to pray, or two bodies lining up in space, the first response is the same: you stop.
Awe often begins right there, with a pause you didn't plan.

how: Muslims may perform a special congregational prayer during a solar or lunar eclipse, following the example described in the hadith; people of different backgrounds gather outdoors with eclipse glasses to watch.

games.q: your son has just died, and the sun goes dark. people around you say the sky is grieving for him. what do you say?
o: yes, the heavens mourn with us.
the sun and moon are signs of God, not eclipsed for anyone's death or life: pray.
say nothing and let them believe it.
games.why: that's what the Prophet Muhammad said, according to the hadith: in his own grief, he turned people from omens to prayer.

practice: Close your eyes and notice the light on your eyelids, then cup your hands over them and stay a few breaths in that small darkness. Lower your hands and let the light come back slowly, the way it does after an eclipse.
If you pray, you can remember God as the light dims, as the hadith describes; if you don't, simply notice the return.

wordCard.voice: An eclipse. The moon crossing the sun: a picture of upheaval for Joel, a sign and a call to prayer in the hadith, and for everyone, a reason to stop. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a solar eclipse; the eclipse prayer is called salat al-kusuf.

carryVoice: Your line: everyone stops. For a few minutes, a dark noon turns strangers into neighbors. Catch you tomorrow.
